items.title: Power and water desalination plant, Kuwait, Kuwait: Kuwait Petroleum Corp reported injuries and significant material damage from repeated Iranian attacks on vital oil sector facilities.
items.description: Kuwait Petroleum Corp reported injuries and significant material damage from repeated Iranian attacks on vital oil sector facilities.
items.rawSummary: Iran struck two power and desalination plants, oil sector facilities, army sites, a Halliburton warehouse, and military bases in Kuwait on July 17–18, causing fires, injuries, and damage, in what ISW-CTP assessed as retaliation for U.S. strikes and a deterrence signal while Kuwait pursues a defense pact with Pakistan.
items.analysis: Iran continued its assault on Kuwaiti critical infrastructure on July 18, striking a second power and desalination plant that sparked a fire, while Kuwait Petroleum Corp reported injuries and significant material damage from repeated attacks on vital oil sector facilities. The strikes follow a July 17 attack that damaged a power generation and water desalination plant, hit army facilities and wounded soldiers, and destroyed a Halliburton logistics warehouse in the Mina Abdullah industrial zone. Subsequent volleys targeted a troop assembly area at Camp Arifjan and a radar system, UAV shelters, and a weapons maintenance hangar at Ali Al Salem airbase. ISW-CTP assessed the infrastructure strikes were likely in response to U.S. strikes on Iranian bridges and a deterrence message after President Trump threatened to expand strikes to power plants; the think tank noted that roughly 90 percent of Kuwait’s drinking water comes from desalination, underscoring the plants' criticality. Amid the widening campaign, Kuwait and Pakistan are in early talks over an expanded defense pact that could include Pakistani support but not combat troop deployments, as ballistic missile impacts rise across the region.

items.description: The Department of Justice announced that federal employees may download TikTok on government devices following an ownership change.
items.rawSummary: Walter Reed National Military Medical Center is treating U.S. military casualties from Operation EPIC FURY amid a wave of presidential actions covering election security declassification, trade tensions with Canada, and a policy change on TikTok for federal employees.
items.analysis: Walter Reed remains the destination for U.S. military casualties requiring continued treatment, with the Department of Defense reporting 13 additional wounded in action from Operation EPIC FURY and medevac flights routing through Ramstein Air Base before transferring patients via Joint Base Andrews. The hospital is operating against a backdrop of intense political activity: President Trump declassified intelligence alleging Chinese and other foreign election interference and accused the intelligence community of withholding information from his briefings, though published files contradict some of his assertions. Clash Report said Trump refused to schedule a meeting with Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu after Netanyahu publicly criticized planned F-35 sales to Turkey. The president also threatened to impose more tariffs on Canada for what he called willful negligence in forest management causing wildfire smoke to drift into the United States. The Trump family media company is reportedly preparing to offer trading firms a millisecond advantage before the president's market-moving Truth Social posts go public, charging a $100,000 monthly fee. Simultaneously, the Pentagon is in talks with SpaceX for compute power under a potential multibillion-dollar deal, according to the Wall Street Journal. In a separate policy shift, the Department of Justice announced that federal employees may now download TikTok on government devices following an ownership change.

items.rawSummary: Walter Reed National Military Medical Center is treating U.S. military casualties from Operation EPIC FURY amid a wave of presidential actions covering election security declassification, trade tensions with Canada, and a policy change on TikTok for federal employees.
items.analysis: Walter Reed remains the destination for U.S. military casualties requiring continued treatment, with the Department of Defense reporting 13 additional wounded in action from Operation EPIC FURY and medevac flights routing through Ramstein Air Base before transferring patients via Joint Base Andrews. The hospital is operating against a backdrop of intense political activity: President Trump declassified intelligence alleging Chinese and other foreign election interference and accused the intelligence community of withholding information from his briefings, though published files contradict some of his assertions. Clash Report said Trump refused to schedule a meeting with Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu after Netanyahu publicly criticized planned F-35 sales to Turkey. The president also threatened to impose more tariffs on Canada for what he called willful negligence in forest management causing wildfire smoke to drift into the United States. The Trump family media company is reportedly preparing to offer trading firms a millisecond advantage before the president's market-moving Truth Social posts go public, charging a $100,000 monthly fee. Simultaneously, the Pentagon is in talks with SpaceX for compute power under a potential multibillion-dollar deal, according to the Wall Street Journal. In a separate policy shift, the Department of Justice announced that federal employees may now download TikTok on government devices following an ownership change.

items.title: Imam Khomeini Hussainiya, Tehran, Iran: The IRGC warned it would target major industrial, information technology, and artificial intelligence assets belonging to companies with US shareholders across the region if U.S. attacks on Iran's bridges and transport infrastructure continue.
items.description: The IRGC warned it would target major industrial, information technology, and artificial intelligence assets belonging to companies with US shareholders across the region if U.S. attacks on Iran's bridges and transport infrastructure continue.
items.rawSummary: Iran's leadership, appearing at Imam Khomeini Hussainiya, escalated defiant rhetoric and threats of offensive action while the IRGC warned it would target regional economic assets with US links in retaliation for continued strikes, as the government intensifies domestic media controls and faces growing internal unrest.
items.analysis: The Hussainiya appearance provided a stage for Iran's leadership to project defiance as U.S. strikes continued across southern Iran, with casualty reports varying from seven dead according to Fars news to 38 killed and over 400 wounded from the Health Ministry. Iran retaliated with strikes on Jordan, Kuwait, and Bahrain, and senior officials warned of expanding the conflict to 'new arenas' while rejecting any diplomatic opening—Parliament Speaker Qalibaf dismissed negotiations, the Foreign Ministry ruled out talks and nuclear concessions, and Foreign Minister Araghchi accused the U.S. of war crimes. Supreme Leader advisor Mohsen Rezaee warned on state TV that Iran would shift from a defensive war to an offensive one if American forces seize any points inside the country, threatening waves of drones and missiles and declaring the 'policy of both war and negotiation is over,' while the IRGC Navy cautioned that U.S. forces were approaching a 'zero hour' and claimed American naval movements under constant surveillance. Late on July 17 the Iranian military claimed to have shot down a US drone, and on the morning of July 18 the IRGC warned it would target major industrial, information technology, and artificial intelligence assets belonging to companies with US shareholders across the region if U.S. attacks on bridges and transport infrastructure continue. These developments unfold alongside a directive ordering media to suppress details of civilian infrastructure damage and service disruptions, while a collapsed rial and reports of an execution tied to 2026 protests underscore the domestic pressure the system is managing.
